claims.text: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has relatively low short-range chemical order.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has pronounced local chemical heterogeneity.
A controlled homogenization treatment will enhance short-range chemical ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Enhanced short-range ordering improves lattice stability.
Enhanced short-range ordering reduces local lattice strain and lattice distortion.
Enhanced short-range ordering creates a more uniform bonding environment.
The more uniform bonding environment limits thermally activated dislocation motion.
Dislocation-mediated plastic deformation is relevant to the elevated-temperature response of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Homogenized specimens will have lower thermal expansion coefficients than as-cast specimens.
Homogenized specimens will have higher elastic moduli than as-cast specimens.
Homogenized specimens will retain yield strength better than as-cast specimens, particularly from about 900 K to 1200 K.
The proposed hypothesis is expected to hold from ambient temperature to approximately 1200 K.
The hypothesis is expected to hold up to about 10% elastic strain.
In situ neutron diffraction can be used at elevated temperature to determine Young's, shear, and bulk moduli.
Thermal expansion coefficients can be obtained from diffraction-measured lattice-parameter shifts.
Diffraction peak profiles can quantitatively establish the degree of short-range ordering in these specimens.
Dislocation density may independently contribute significantly to the observed mechanical responses.
The controlled comparison is between as-cast and homogenized HfNbTaTiZr specimens tested under otherwise matched high-temperature tensile and diffraction conditions.

contradictions.description: The boundary describes strains up to about 10% as elastic, while the proposed measurements include yielding, work hardening, dislocation evolution, and plastic stress–strain behavior. Those measurements require a post-yield plastic regime, so the stated elastic-strain boundary is inconsistent with the planned test.
